blocks.text: A 62-year-old man with long-standing diabetes feels faint every time he gets out of a chair. His blood pressure drops from 140/85 mmHg lying to 100/60 mmHg standing, yet his pulse stays at 70 beats per minute in both positions. A healthy heart would have sped up. Something in his reflex loop has failed.

blocks.markdown:
**The baroreceptor reflex** is a rapid negative-feedback loop that holds arterial pressure steady from second to second. **Baroreceptors** are stretch-sensitive free nerve endings in the walls of the **carotid sinus** (afferents in the **glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX**) and **aortic arch** (afferents in the **vagus nerve, CN X**). They fire in proportion to arterial wall stretch, so firing rises when pressure rises and falls when it falls.

Afferents synapse in the **nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)** of the medulla. A rise in firing excites the **caudal ventrolateral medulla**, which inhibits the **rostral ventrolateral medulla** (the tonic drive to sympathetic preganglionic neurones), and excites vagal neurones in the **nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus**. The result is **lower sympathetic output and higher vagal output**: heart rate and vessel tone fall, pulling pressure back down. A fall in pressure produces the opposite response.

blocks.title: Mean arterial pressure
blocks.text: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the time-averaged pressure that drives perfusion. At resting heart rates it is approximated by diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure, where pulse pressure = systolic minus diastolic.

blocks.title: Standing up in a healthy adult
blocks.prompt: A healthy adult stands from lying. Supine BP is 120/80 mmHg. Describe the sequence of events and compute the supine MAP.

steps.text: On standing, gravity pools blood in the veins of the legs and splanchnic bed, so venous return, stroke volume, cardiac output and arterial pressure fall transiently.
Baroreceptor stretch decreases, so afferent firing in CN IX and X falls; NTS output reduces inhibition of the rostral ventrolateral medulla and reduces vagal drive.
Sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls: heart rate and contractility rise, arterioles and veins constrict, restoring pressure within seconds.
Supine MAP: pulse pressure 120 - 80 = 40; one third = 13.3; MAP = 80 + 13.3 = 93.3 mmHg.

blocks.answer: Reflex sympathetic activation and vagal withdrawal restore pressure; supine MAP is about 93 mmHg.

rows: Stretch receptors in carotid sinus and aortic arch
CN IX (carotid sinus), CN X (aortic arch)

blocks.markdown:
**Micturition (bladder control).** During **filling**, the bladder accommodates urine at low pressure. Sympathetic fibres from **T10-L2** travel in the **hypogastric nerves**; they relax the detrusor (beta-3) and contract the internal urethral sphincter (alpha-1). **Somatic motor fibres** from **S2-S4** (the **Onuf nucleus**) travel in the **pudendal nerve** to contract the **external urethral sphincter**, which is skeletal muscle under voluntary control. Afferents travel in the pelvic nerves.

As the bladder fills, stretch afferents signal the **pontine micturition centre**, which, when social conditions permit, switches on **voiding**: **parasympathetic fibres from S2-S4** in the **pelvic splanchnic nerves** contract the detrusor (muscarinic M3) and relax the internal sphincter, while pudendal output to the external sphincter is inhibited. Voluntary control depends on the frontal cortex and connections to the pontine centre.

blocks.title: Why damage to the sacral roots impairs emptying
blocks.prompt: Explain why compression of the S2-S4 roots in the cauda equina leads to urinary retention.

steps.text: The motor drive to the detrusor travels in S2-S4 parasympathetic fibres; interrupting them removes the signal to contract.
The detrusor becomes underactive, so the bladder fills and cannot empty.
Sensation of fullness is also reduced, so the bladder may overdistend; pressure eventually exceeds the sphincter's resistance, causing overflow incontinence.

blocks.answer: Loss of S2-S4 parasympathetic motor and sensory function causes an atonic bladder with retention and overflow.

blocks.markdown: **Autonomic failure.** The baroreflex requires an intact afferent limb, brainstem integration and an efferent limb. When the **efferent sympathetic** limb fails (autonomic neuropathy in diabetes, pure autonomic failure, multiple system atrophy, Parkinson disease, some drugs), standing cannot trigger vasoconstriction, so pressure falls and stays down. The heart rate also fails to rise (a **fixed heart rate**). **Orthostatic (postural) hypotension** is conventionally defined as a sustained fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. Symptoms include dizziness, visual dimming and syncope. In contrast, if hypotension results from **hypovolaemia** and the reflex is intact, heart rate rises markedly.

blocks.title: Reflex intact or failed?
blocks.text: Check the heart rate response. A large rise in pulse with a fall in pressure suggests volume depletion with an intact reflex. A fall in pressure without a pulse rise suggests failure of the autonomic reflex.

points: The baroreceptor reflex senses pressure in the carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X), integrates in the NTS and medulla, and adjusts sympathetic and vagal output.
On standing, reduced baroreceptor firing increases sympathetic and decreases vagal output, raising heart rate and vascular tone.
Bladder filling is sympathetic (T10-L2) plus pudendal; voiding is parasympathetic (S2-S4) with pontine coordination.
Autonomic failure impairs the efferent limb, causing postural hypotension without a compensatory rise in heart rate.

questions.stem: Which nerve carries afferent signals from the carotid sinus baroreceptors to the brainstem?

distractorRationale.a: The vagus carries aortic arch baroreceptor afferents.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the carotid sinus nerve is a branch of CN IX.
distractorRationale.c: CN XII is motor to the tongue.
distractorRationale.d: CN V is not involved in baroreception.

questions.explanation: Carotid sinus afferents travel in the sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, to the nucleus tractus solitarius. Aortic arch baroreceptors use the vagus.

questions.stem: Baroreceptor afferents terminate first in which brainstem structure?

distractorRationale.a: The red nucleus is a motor relay of the midbrain.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the NTS in the medulla receives visceral afferents.
distractorRationale.c: The substantia nigra is part of the basal ganglia circuit.
distractorRationale.d: The inferior olive projects to the cerebellum.

questions.explanation: The nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla receives baroreceptor afferents and projects to medullary centres that adjust sympathetic and vagal output.

questions.stem: Firm pressure over the carotid sinus in an older man produces a slower pulse and a fall in blood pressure. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Increased stretch of the baroreceptors raises firing, which reduces sympathetic and increases vagal output
Reduced baroreceptor firing, which increases sympathetic output
Direct block of the sinoatrial node

questions.correctOptionText: Increased stretch of the baroreceptors raises firing, which reduces sympathetic and increases vagal output

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pressure mimics a rise in arterial pressure.
distractorRationale.b: Reduced firing would raise heart rate and pressure.
distractorRationale.c: The effect is reflex-mediated via the brainstem, not a direct block.
distractorRationale.d: The Cushing reflex involves raised intracranial pressure.

questions.explanation: Pressure deforms the sinus wall, the baroreceptors fire as if pressure were high, and the reflex reduces sympathetic drive and raises vagal tone. Heart rate and blood pressure fall.

questions.stem: After standing, a patient's blood pressure is 108/72 mmHg. Using MAP = diastolic + one third of pulse pressure, what is the MAP in mmHg?
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure = 108 - 72 = 36 mmHg and one third is 12 mmHg. MAP = 72 + 12 = 84 mmHg.

questions.stem: Which nerve carries the parasympathetic motor fibres that contract the detrusor muscle during voiding?

distractorRationale.a: The hypogastric nerve carries sympathetic fibres.
distractorRationale.b: The pudendal nerve supplies the external sphincter.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: S2-S4 pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic fibres to the detrusor.
distractorRationale.d: The genitofemoral nerve is a somatic nerve of the inguinal region.

questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry S2-S4 parasympathetic efferents that contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter during voiding.

questions.stem: Which structure provides voluntary control of urinary continence by contracting skeletal muscle and is supplied by S2-S4?

options.text: External urethral sphincter, via the pudendal nerve

questions.correctOptionText: External urethral sphincter, via the pudendal nerve

distractorRationale.a: The detrusor is smooth muscle controlled by the autonomic system.
distractorRationale.b: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle and autonomic.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the external sphincter is skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve from the Onuf nucleus.

questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter is striated muscle supplied by somatic motor neurones of the Onuf nucleus (S2-S4) in the pudendal nerve. It is the only voluntary component of continence.

questions.stem: True or false: during voiding the parasympathetic system contracts the detrusor and the internal urethral sphincter relaxes.
questions.explanation: Voiding is a parasympathetic event: S2-S4 outflow contracts the detrusor and opens the internal sphincter while the external sphincter is inhibited. Sympathetic activity dominates during storage.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with Parkinson disease has a lying BP of 145/85 mmHg and a standing BP of 100/60 mmHg after 2 minutes, with heart rate 68 and 70 beats/min respectively. Which interpretation is most consistent?

options.text: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension due to failure of reflex sympathetic vasoconstriction

questions.correctOptionText: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension due to failure of reflex sympathetic vasoconstriction

distractorRationale.a: With hypovolaemia and an intact reflex the heart rate would rise substantially.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a large fall in BP with almost no rise in heart rate indicates a failed autonomic reflex.
distractorRationale.c: Heart rate is not unusually slow, and the problem is vascular.
distractorRationale.d: A fall of 45 mmHg systolic is not normal.

questions.explanation: The drop exceeds the 20/10 mmHg criteria, and the pulse barely changes, which means the reflex efferent limb is not responding. This pattern is typical of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension seen in autonomic failure.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with pure autonomic failure, caused by degeneration of postganglionic sympathetic neurones, faints on standing. Explain the mechanism, and how the heart rate response helps distinguish her condition from hypovolaemia.
markingGuide: Standing pools blood in the legs, reducing venous return and arterial pressure
Normally baroreceptor unloading increases sympathetic output and decreases vagal tone
Degeneration of postganglionic sympathetic neurones means the efferent limb fails, so sympathetic vasoconstriction and cardioacceleration cannot be generated
Pressure falls and remains low, causing dizziness or syncope
Heart rate shows little or no rise (fixed rate)
In hypovolaemia the reflex is intact so heart rate rises markedly
questions.explanation: In autonomic failure the baroreflex efferent limb cannot constrict vessels or speed the heart, so the pressure fall on standing is uncorrected. Because the reflex is intact in hypovolaemia, tachycardia accompanies the fall in pressure there.

questions.stem: Describe the neural control of the bladder in an adult who is storing urine at a social gathering and then voids voluntarily 20 minutes later. Name the nerves, spinal levels and the roles of the detrusor and the two sphincters in each phase.
markingGuide: Storage: sympathetic outflow (T10-L2, hypogastric nerve) relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal sphincter
Pudendal nerve (S2-S4, Onuf nucleus) keeps the external sphincter contracted, under voluntary control
Stretch afferents signal fullness to the brainstem and cortex
Voiding: pontine micturition centre activates S2-S4 parasympathetic neurones in the pelvic splanchnic nerves
Detrusor contracts and the internal sphincter relaxes
Pudendal output to the external sphincter is inhibited so it relaxes
questions.explanation: Storage is maintained by sympathetic and somatic output that keep the detrusor relaxed and the sphincters closed. Voiding switches this pattern under control of the pontine micturition centre, using parasympathetic drive to contract the detrusor while the sphincters relax.
